change orchistration so that it is optimised for cost, summarise the content of each agent and pass that to the orchistrator, use sonnet-5 as the default model and opus-5 for the trch lead and BA only. The dominant cost in swarm coding is tokens, and in a swarm the token bill is mostly context, not output. Each sub-agent re-reads files, re-loads instructions, and re-explains state. So most of your savings come from controlling what context each agent sees, not from picking a cheaper model. In rough priority order:

Tier your models. Don't run everything on your most capable model. Route by task difficulty: a cheap/fast model for mechanical work (renaming, boilerplate, running tests, summarizing diffs, file search), a mid model for most implementation, and the expensive model only for planning, hard debugging, and final review. A good orchestrator does the routing decision on a small model too. This alone is often a 5–10x swing.

Exploit prompt caching aggressively. Put stable content — system prompt, repo conventions, the files an agent needs — at the front of the context so it hits the cache across turns and across agents. Keep the volatile part (the specific task) at the end. Cached input tokens are roughly a tenth the price, so structuring prompts for cache hits matters more than almost anything else.

Keep sub-agents narrow and short-lived. The expensive failure mode is an agent that accumulates a huge context over 40 turns exploring the whole repo. Give each agent a tight scope, only the files it needs, and a hard turn/token budget. Have it return a compact result (a diff and a one-paragraph summary) rather than its full transcript. The orchestrator should never inherit a sub-agent's raw context — just its distilled output.

Don't fan out redundantly. Parallel agents are only worth it when the work is genuinely independent. Spawning three agents to "try different approaches" and picking the best triples your cost for the winner plus two you throw away — only do that on high-value, uncertain tasks. For most work, decompose into non-overlapping units so agents don't re-solve each other's problems.

Gate expensive steps behind cheap ones. Run linters, type checkers, and the test suite (deterministic, free) before you spend model tokens on review. Fail fast: if compilation breaks, don't call a model to reason about downstream behavior. Use a cheap model as a first-pass filter and escalate to the expensive one only when the cheap one is uncertain.

Cut context re-reading. Maintain a shared, compact artifact of repo state (file map, key interfaces, decisions made) that agents read instead of re-exploring. Have agents work from diffs and targeted file reads rather than dumping whole directories into context.

Instrument cost per task. Log tokens per agent per task type so you can see where the money actually goes — it's usually one or two agent roles or one runaway loop, and it's rarely where you'd guess.
